title: A hundred pounds of myrrh (John 19:38–42)
hookLine: Nicodemus, who came by night, comes by day with spices

lines: ONE BRIEF WORD IN CHAPTER SEVEN.
cards: Way back in chapter three, a man came to Jesus at night. Nicodemus: a Pharisee, a leader, a respected teacher.
He asked careful questions about being born from above, and the last John gives of him that night is puzzled: how can these things be?
In chapter seven, he spoke up once, briefly, saying the law should give a man a hearing. Then he dropped out of the story. Now Jesus is dead.
Peter, the loudest of the followers, is nowhere in this scene. And two quiet men walk forward, in daylight, to do what nobody else will.

teach.h: JOSEPH, A SECRET DISCIPLE, ASKS PILATE.
teach.b: The first is Joseph of Arimathea. John says he was a disciple, "but secretly for fear of the Jews."
In John's Gospel that phrase usually means the religious authorities, and the other Gospels say Joseph sat on their council. Now he goes to Pilate himself and asks for the body. That's a public act.
Then the second man. In the King James Bible: "And there came also Nicodemus, which at the first came to Jesus by night, and brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight."

teach.h: A HUNDRED POUNDS: A ROYAL AMOUNT?
teach.b: A hundred pounds. John's pound, the Roman litra, was lighter than a modern pound, but even so, that's an enormous amount of spice. The Hebrew Bible tells of a king of Judah laid in a bed filled with spices.
Some readers see Nicodemus and Joseph giving Jesus a royal burial, for the King of the Jews, as Pilate's sign said. They wrap the body in linen with the spices, as John says was the Jewish custom.

teach.h: A NEW TOMB IN A GARDEN.
teach.b: Nearby is a garden, and in it a new tomb where no one had ever been laid. The Sabbath is coming, so there they lay him. Notice the arc of this man's story.
By night in chapter three. One brief word in chapter seven.

teach.h: WHICH AT THE FIRST CAME TO JESUS BY NIGHT.
teach.b: Now by day, carrying something heavy, in front of everyone. John never tells us what Nicodemus believed in the end. Tradition makes him a saint.
The text simply shows a man coming slowly into the light.

how: Christians remember Jesus's burial on Holy Saturday, a day of quiet waiting in many churches, and Orthodox Christians honor Joseph and Nicodemus among the myrrh-bearers on the second Sunday after Easter.

o: the rich man who gave his own tomb for Jesus
the disciple who ran first to the empty tomb
the Pharisee who came by night, then by day

games.q: what's inside John 19:38–42 — tap the pairs.

s: Nicodemus appears only once in John's Gospel
three times: by night in chapter 3, briefly in chapter 7, and here at the burial.
the Hebrew Bible tells of a king laid in a bed of spices
King Asa, in 2 Chronicles 16:14. some readers see a royal burial in Nicodemus's hundred pounds.
John tells us what Nicodemus believed at the end
he doesn't. the text shows what he did, not what he said.

games.q: you're Nicodemus. you once came to Jesus at night so no one would see. now he's dead, and his loud followers are hiding. what do you do?
o: bring a hundred pounds of spices and help bury him, in daylight.
send a servant with a small gift.
games.why: he comes himself, openly, with myrrh and aloes, "about an hundred pound weight."

practice: Think of someone you care about, or a cause, a belief, your faith or your questions, that you've kept a little quiet. You don't have to make a speech; just picture one small way to carry your care into the daylight.
If you pray, ask for some of Nicodemus's courage.

wordCard.voice: Nicodemus. The Pharisee who first came to Jesus by night, and now returns in daylight with a hundred pounds of myrrh.

orig.note: Greek: a hundred litrai, Roman pounds, each lighter than a modern pound.

carryVoice: Your line: in daylight now. Slowly, and still into the light, where care can be seen. Until tomorrow.
